etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English chewen, from Old English ċēowan, from Proto-West Germanic *keuwan, from Proto-Germanic *kewwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵyewh₁-. Cognate with West Frisian kôgje, Low German käwwen, Dutch kauwen, German kauen; also Latin gingīva (“gums”), Tocharian B śuwaṃ (“to eat”), Polish żuć (“to chew”), Persian جویدن (javidan), Pashto ژول (žovạl, “to bite, gnaw”).

definitions.definition: To crush with the teeth by repeated closing and opening of the jaws; done to food to soften it and break it down by the action of saliva before it is swallowed.

quote.text: The same chewn upon maketh one to avoid much phlegm.

And gruesome they areː We find cattle still alive with hindquarters chewn off, still alive with their eyes chewn out, their ears chewn off, their noses and faces chewn till they look like (a) Hamburger, their tails hanging in shreds. Or, we find them after a slow and cruel death. Can you understand why cattlemen will shoot YOUR dog if he is seen wandering on ranchland?

quote.citation: 1976, Denis Diderot, translated by Leonard Tancock, Rameau's Nephew / D'alembert's Dream‎[1]:
quote.text: But meanwhile Mademoiselle's book had at least been found under an arm-chair where it had been dragged, chewn up and torn to pieces by a young pug-dog or by a kitten.

quote.citation: 2001, Keith Douglass, Seal Team Seven 14: Death Blow‎[2]:
quote.text: He wore two sweaters, both moth chewn and filthy but warm.

quote.citation: 2010, Tony Reynolds, The Lost Stories of Sherlock Holmes‎[3]:
quote.text: His left cheek seemed to have been cut and chewn awayǃ

definitions.definition: To grind, tear, or otherwise degrade or demolish something with teeth or as with teeth.
(informal) To think about something; to ponder; to chew over.

quote.text: Old politicians chew on wisdom past.

quote.citation: 1711, Matthew Prior, to Mr. Harley, wounded by Guiscard:
quote.text: He chews revenge, abjuring his offense.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English chew, cheu, icheu, from Old English *ċēaw, *ġeċēaw (“chewing”), from Proto-West Germanic *kauw, *gakauw (“chewing”), from Proto-Germanic *kewwaną (“to chew”). Cognate with obsolete Dutch kauw (“chewing”), Dutch gekauw (“chewing”), West Frisian gekau (“chewing”).

definitions.definition: The act of chewing; mastication with the mouth.

definitions.definition: A small sweet, such as a taffy, that is eaten by chewing.
(countable) A plug or wad of chewing tobacco; chaw or a chaw.
(uncountable, informal) The condition of something being torn or ground up mechanically.
